item.title: Higher-Order Functions Are Not Free: The reduce That's Secretly O(n²)
item.description:
map, filter, and reduce get recommended as the faster choice over a for loop. They do read better. Faster is the part that does not hold up, and one of them has a default that turns a one-line accumulation into O(n²) while sailing through review. By the end you will know which one, why, and the one-word change that fixes it.

“Functional is faster” is backwards more often than not

A for loop over an array is about as cheap as computing gets: one pass, one array, no intermediates. A chain of higher-order functions does the same logical work and allocates along the way.

item.title: How Closures Capture, and Why Your Screen Leaks
item.description: Push a screen, pop it, push it again, and watch deinit never fire while memory climbs. That is the most common memory bug in iOS, and it almost always comes down to one thing a closure does quietly: capture. A closure grabs the things it references and keeps them alive. Get that wrong with a closure that outlives the call, and you have a view controller that can never deallocate.

item.title: The Hidden Cost of Value Types: Copy-on-Write, and When Structs Bite
item.description:
“Use structs by default” is advice so repeated that nobody asks the obvious follow-up: what does the copy actually cost? Everyone can recite that structs copy and classes share. The part worth your attention is what “copy” means at runtime, when it is free, when it quietly is not, and the class of bug that shows up when you have lost track of which one you are holding.

We will assume you know the textbook difference. Assign a struct, you get an independent copy. Assign a class, both names point at the same instance. Here is everything past that.

item.title: What Swift's Optional Really Is, and When to Stop Reaching for It
item.description:
How many states can a screen actually be in, and does its type let it represent states that mean nothing? That question is where optionals stop being about syntax.

Everyone meets Optional once, as “the box that might be empty,” then moves on to unwrapping. The parts that still bite years in are elsewhere: what Optional actually is, the two or three places it behaves in ways that surprise people, and the design call nobody frames at the syntax stage. When is an optional the right tool, and when is it a sign the problem has not been modeled yet?
